newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey threatens Cyprus over missile crisis.
newsitem.headline: Turkey threatens Cyprus over missile crisis.

text.p: Turkey is seriously considering staging a military strike if Cyprus goes ahead with plans to deploy Russian anti-aircraft missiles on the divided island, the state-run Anatolian news agency reported on Thursday.
"Ankara is seriously considering an operation against the missile launchers when the time comes if Turkey's warnings to the Greek Cypriot administration are not heeded," the agency said.

Turkey has accused the Cypriot government of trying to change the balance of forces on Cyprus with a deal announced last weekend to buy Russian S-300 surface-to-air missiles that could neutralise Turkish air superiority on the island.
It is unclear when the missiles will be delivered.
The Cypriot government says the missiles are defensive. The S-300 air defence system has a range of 150 km (90 miles) and can knock out aircraft and missiles in flight.

Turkey invaded Cyprus in 1974 in response to a Greek Cypriot coup inspired by the military then ruling Athens. Around 30,000 troops occupy northern Cyprus, which declared itself a Turkish Cypriot state in 1983 but is recognised only by Ankara.

Western governments fear the missile row, coupled with recent killings in the U.N.-patrolled buffer zone dividing Cyprus, could reignite old conflicts between fellow NATO members Greece and Turkey. Athens is committed to the defence of the internationally recognised Cyprus government in the Greek Cypriot-controlled south of the Mediterranean island.
The United States warned Turkey on Thursday against launching any attack on Cyprus.

"This is no time for the Turkish government to be making wild and dramatic statements which will not be supported by any sensisble member of the international community. It would be completely out of bounds for Turkey to take this action," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said in Washington.
The Cypriot government dismissed the threats of a military strike by Turkey as nothing new.

"For us the matter is over," Foreign Minister Alecos Michaelides told Reuters. "We will not follow Turkey with polemic statements. We are focusing our attention to the political solution of the problem."
Earlier on Thursday the Greek governnment shrugged off similar but less explicit threats by Turkey.

Prime Minister Costas Simitis said Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides would be invited to Athens for talks on the issue this month but added there was no cause for concern that a new crisis would erupt between Greece and Turkey.

"There is nothing new in our region. Turkish aggression has been expressed for some time," he told reporters. "We would be playing Turkey's game if we showed particular worry over this and were swept into an atmosphere of crisis."

The Cypriot government has refused to yield to international pressure -- namely from Washington -- to cancel the missile deal, saying they are necessary to defend the island in the event of a Turkish attack.
Earlier Turkish Defence Minister Turhan Tayan said Turkey would use all possible means to halt the missile deployment.

"We are strongly against these missiles going to the island. We will use all our capabilities to prevent it," Tayan was quoted as saying by Anatolian. "They will be used when the time is right in the necessary manner and proportion."
The agency said Tayan drew a parallel with the Cuban missile crisis in 1962 when Russia tried to deploy missiles on Cuba.
"Those who play with fire have to take the responsibilities for their actions," Tayan said.
